doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 9, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Growing up on the Basie bus
summary: Butch says life on the Basie band matured him and that only Buddy Rich and Muhammad Ali could back up their boasts.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: It is. You’re absolutely right about that. I learned so much, and I did so much growing up on that bus and those one-nighters, and those stages and gig after gig after gig and meeting people, myriads of different folks from all walks of life who either loved the music or hated the music. It was okay because it was just the experience. I did an awful lot of growing up and that was my experience with the band. And I’m still growing. I find myself now thinking about things I did 30 years ago and I realize I could have handled it better. Because now I’ve gone through a lot more than what I had before. I wasn’t that savvy or even that civilized early on, let’s face it, Monk. I was a smart-ass. You know? I’d get off the stage and someone would say something like, “Man that was a great set.” And I’d say, “Yeah it was.” Why would I do that? Because I was being, you know, the smart ass. Instead of saying thank you very much, which I do now. I appreciate it if someone likes my playing or if someone likes the music, “Thank you very much.” I worked very hard to get to do that and I’m glad that you can hear that. I’m glad I can do that for you. But you know that, yeah I can really play, man, you ought to hear me play a shuffle, oh man. Monk Rowe ain’t heard nothing yet ‘til I play my shuffle. No. You know? I’ve only heard in my entire life two people that would say something that was outrageous and then back it up completely. And those two people were Buddy Rich and Muhammad Ali. Outside of that you’ve got to take everybody’s pronouncements with a grain of salt.
